title: The Salt Crisis That Sent a Negev Kibbutz into Making Drippers
dek: In 1965, with its farming failing on salty desert soil, Kibbutz Hatzerim made a small, resellable bet on Simcha Blass's drip irrigation.

story.founder: Simcha Blass, Uri Werber and Kibbutz Hatzerim
story.event: Kibbutz Hatzerim turning from failing farming to manufacture Simcha Blass's drip emitters
story.summary: In the mid-1960s Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev was failing at farming because of water shortage and salty soil, and its members decided they needed an industry linked to agriculture that would employ about fourteen people. Member Uri Werber met the water engineer Simcha Blass, who had developed and patented a plastic drip emitter; an agreement was signed in August 1965 and Netafim was set up in January 1966 with a small investment in an existing building. In 1972 the company brought in engineer Rafi Mehoudar to improve the drippers, and by 2015 it sold in about 110 countries.
paragraphs: In 1964 Naty Barak left Haifa for Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev desert, one of a group of young people who meant to farm there. It was not working. Water was short and the soil was salty; Uri Werber, a member, later recalled what they called the "salt crisis", when layers of salt were found in the kibbutz's land. Barak remembered worrying, too, that the founders could not keep up such hard physical work for long. "We came to an agreement that we needed industry," Werber said.

They set rules, Barak recalled: the business should be connected to agriculture, should not need much labour, and should give work to fourteen members. Werber had heard of Simcha Blass, a veteran water engineer behind the pipeline from the Sea of Galilee to the southern desert, and met him in 1964. Decades earlier Blass had noticed one tree thriving beside a pipe that leaked drop by drop. Once cheap plastic arrived he experimented with drippers in his backyard, worked with his son, and patented an emitter.

The technology was new, and Werber later stressed how little the kibbutz put at stake. It made a small initial investment and used an empty industrial building that already had electricity and water; the equipment could have been sold if the venture failed. "There was a risk, but it wasn't big," he said. An agreement with Blass was signed in August 1965, and Netafim, Hebrew for droplets, was set up in January 1966. Within six to eight months, Werber said, he could see it would succeed.

It was not smooth. Werber thought Blass's drippers innovative but not quite good enough, and in 1972 the company approached Rafi Mehoudar, a young engineer who designed pressure regulators for sprinklers. He told them, "I don't know what agriculture is, I don't know what a kibbutz is, I don't know what a dripper is." They taught him and gave him a wish-list: drippers that coped with changes in pressure and temperature and did not clog. Farmers in many countries resisted the new method. "Slowly, slowly we advanced," Werber said. By 2015 Netafim sold in about 110 countries; he had hoped only for a factory that succeeded "in Israeli terms".

quote.text: A great man is always willing to be little. Whilst he sits on the cushion of advantages, he goes to sleep. When he is pushed, tormented, defeated, he has a chance to learn something
quote.source_title: Essays — First Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2944
quote.connection: Emerson credits adversity: the comfortable sleep, the pushed learn. The salt crisis did push Hatzerim. But Werber's own account stresses a different instinct, a bet kept small enough to sell off if it failed, and that caution may have mattered as much as the pressure did.

reflection: It is easy to tell this as a story of bold invention in the desert. Werber told it more modestly: the farming was failing, so they tried something, and they kept the stake small enough that failure would not have ruined them. An empty building, equipment that could be resold, fourteen jobs as the goal.

Emerson is right that pressure teaches. But pressure is not the same as recklessness, and you are allowed to answer a hard season with a careful experiment rather than a leap. When you weigh your next step, it is fair to ask not only what could go right, but what you could keep or walk away with if it does not.
invitation: Take one decision you are weighing this week and write down what it would cost you if it failed. If that cost is bearable, let yourself try a smaller version of it rather than waiting.

cross_checks.claim: Netafim was founded at Kibbutz Hatzerim in 1965 around Simcha Blass's drip emitter
The kibbutz turned to industry because farming was failing on salty soil with too little water
The venture was meant to employ about fourteen kibbutz members
Blass's idea came from a tree thriving beside a slowly leaking water source, and he later developed a plastic emitter
Blass's original drippers were improved by a later engineer (Rafi Mehoudar, from 1972)

research_notes: Dates: Netafim and most accounts give 1965 as the founding year; Werber told the Jerusalem Post the agreement with Blass was signed in August 1965 and Netafim was established in January 1966. The story gives both. Blass's tree observation: Barak dates it to the late 1930s and describes a row of trees with one larger beside a cracked pipe; JTA places it in the early 1930s and describes a big tree fed by underground water. The story says only 'decades earlier' and 'one tree'. The kibbutz's problem: Barak cites water shortage and high salinity, Werber the 'salt crisis'; the story uses both. Barak said the founders were 'probably in their late thirties' and that the kibbutz members thought them old at the time; the story says only that they could not keep up the physical work for long. The terms of the 1965 deal (often given as 80 per cent kibbutz, 20 per cent Blass, plus a royalty) appear only in Wikipedia and an unreachable magazine excerpt, so the story leaves the terms out; funding is set to mixed because the kibbutz's own investment and Blass's patent and stake both went into it. The Jerusalem Post article body is served in the page's structured data; its visible text loads with a script. Netafim's later ownership (majority sold to Mexichem, later Orbia, in the late 2010s, with the kibbutz keeping a stake) is left out because sources give 2017 and 2018. Country count: Maidan gave about 110 countries in 2015; Jüdische Allgemeine says more than 100 today; the story uses the 2015 figure. Barak was not a founder of the company but a kibbutz member who joined in 1964 and later served as Netafim's chief sustainability officer; his recollections are attributed to him.
